title: Carnival of Souls

evidence.note: Wikipedia reports that the film's US release lacked a valid copyright notice, which would put it in the US public domain, and that the foreign release carried a copyright card protecting overseas sales. No primary record (Copyright Office catalog search or Catalog of Copyright Entries renewal volume for the 28th-year window) was fetched in this session, so the layer is held at undetermined.
The Internet Archive hosts the film (item CarnivalofSouls) and tags it Public Domain.

Gene Moore wrote an original organ score for the film. As a sound film, the recorded track would normally share the print's status, which is itself unconfirmed by a primary record. No separate registration or renewal was checked.
John Clifford wrote the screenplay, completing it in three weeks. No pre-existing underlying work was identified, but no primary record was checked.

No active mark was identified, but no trademark database was searched. The 1998 remake, Wes Craven Presents Carnival of Souls, was made under rights acquired from Herk Harvey and John Clifford and is a separate work.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected, such as a newly composed or recorded score, new titles or subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.

Criterion released a 2-disc DVD in 2000 with a 78-minute theatrical version and an 84-minute director's cut, then reissued the film on DVD and Blu-ray in 2016 with a new restoration. Any added commentary, subtitles or other original material on those discs may be protected.

editorial:
Carnival of Souls was made for about $33,000, with $17,000 raised from local investors at $500 per share. Herk Harvey directed it from a John Clifford screenplay, with an original organ score by Gene Moore. It opened on September 26, 1962 at the Granada Theatre in Lawrence, Kansas. A reuser wants it because the US release is reported to have lacked a valid copyright notice, and the Internet Archive hosts a copy tagged Public Domain.

The trap is that this status rests on a secondary source. Wikipedia also reports that the foreign release carried a copyright card protecting overseas sales. This dossier did not check the Copyright Office catalog or the renewal records, so every layer stays undetermined except restorations. Criterion's 2016 restoration and its discs may carry protectable additions, and ripping a copy-protected disc can raise a DMCA issue. If you use the film, use the Internet Archive copy.
faq: Can I upload or reuse Carnival of Souls?

The US release is reported to have lacked a valid copyright notice, but no primary record was checked here, so treat the status as unconfirmed. The Internet Archive copy is the safest source. Avoid ripping Criterion discs, which may include protected additions and copy protection.
Is the 1998 remake also public domain?
No. Wes Craven Presents Carnival of Souls is a separate work made under rights acquired from Herk Harvey and John Clifford.
